prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and showing how reallocation across firms shapes who exports, who invests abroad and how countries gain from trade

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B001 alone, with Melitz and Helpman. What I did in this round was test it against the strongest objections instead of relying on the fact that all eleven round-1 files converge. The chair summary itself warns that convergence among files from the same model may reflect shared reasoning patterns, and that the count is not a merit argument. The case on content is as follows. Melitz (2003) and Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (2004) moved trade analysis from representative firms and sectors to reallocation across heterogeneous firms. That produced a selection and reallocation channel for the gains from trade, a sharp exports-versus-FDI sorting result, and a firm-level empirical agenda that is now routine. The framework is also used in macro and growth work on productivity and reallocation, which I know from my own field of quantitative general-equilibrium modelling. The core papers are more than twenty years old and have been tested and extended in many countries' firm data. The credit traces to a short list of papers: Melitz for the selection model, and Helpman, with Melitz and Yeaple, for the sorting result, building on his earlier monopolistic-competition trade theory. On the chair's questions, my answers are these. (1) The omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum should be acknowledged in the scientific background and handled by keeping the citation to the theoretical selection mechanism. The Committee can only credit names on the ballot entry, and I do not think the omission makes a two-name award indefensible, though it is the main residual risk. (2) I read the discovery as selection and reallocation, not as the whole firm-level or quantitative-trade programme. (3) On the common criterion, I weigh a change in what a field theorises and how it measures its central question at least as much as a change in how it estimates. I do not treat that as a rule that excludes toolkits, and B006 remains a legitimate fallback. (4) I do not propose a two-part prize. B001 uses two of the three permitted people. The only way to add B006 is to credit a single person such as Pakes, which would split the BLP credit and misrepresent the discovery, and I would rather not do that just to fill a slot. (5) The citation should not claim settled welfare magnitudes, since the baseline model's welfare results depend on distributional assumptions.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related contributions, including the exporter-premia facts and the Ricardian-heterogeneity lineage, and none is credited on this entry. Redding's quantitative and spatial work is excluded. A two-name prize can be read as under-crediting the empirical and quantitative strands that made the framework operational, and Enflo is right that whether this is acceptable depends on a judgement about what counts as the discovery, which the record does not settle. Part of the new-trade-theory lineage was recognised in 2008, and Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition work sits close to it. The baseline Melitz model's sharper predictions are rejected in detail, and its welfare implications depend on functional-form and distributional assumptions. B001 is also theory-led, with a more indirect link to day-to-day policy practice than B006's use in antitrust and merger review. If the Committee decides the credit boundary for B001 is too entangled, B006 limited to the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes demand-estimation core is my fallback.

responses.point: Enflo is less comfortable than others in treating the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as only a caveat. If the discovery is read as the empirical facts plus the theory, the ballot's credited names would be incomplete. She also says the citation should name selection and firm heterogeneity and say nothing generic about trade theory.
responses.response: I agree with the citation point and have tightened my wording so that it names selection, reallocation and the exports-versus-FDI sorting result, not trade theory in general. On attribution I accept that this is a judgement and not a finding. My reading is that the prize recognises the model that organised the empirical facts and produced a new welfare channel, and that the exporter-premia facts motivated and tested the theory but did not supply the selection mechanism. I would not hide the gap. The Scientific Background should state plainly that the empirical precursors and parallel lineages are outside the credit. If the Committee reads the discovery as the combined empirical-and-theoretical programme, my case for the two-name award weakens, and that is the condition under which I would move toward B006.

responses.point: Strömberg has moved B006 from first to alternative because the boundary between BLP demand estimation and the dynamic-games strand is unclear, and Bresnahan's independent contributions cannot all be credited within three names. He also says that if the Committee wants to cover the full firm-level trade lineage, the two-name award is vulnerable.
responses.response: I share your reading of both points, and our moves from the opening came from the same reasoning. I put the discovery-boundary problem of B006 to the Committee as a question, and your answer helps: a B006 prize would have to choose explicitly between the demand-estimation core and the broader structural-IO toolkit. I do not think a narrow BLP prize is unacceptable. It is the cleanest fallback I see. But it would leave out Pakes's dynamic-industry work, Bresnahan and Reiss as separate contributions, and the entry-model strand, and that is a real cost. I also agree that B001 is exposed if the lineage is drawn broadly. I think a narrow citation is the honest answer to that exposure, not a reason to enlarge the credited set beyond what the ballot entry supports.

responses.point: Boppart did not rank B034 in his top eight because of thematic overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, and because the empirical identification of the collateral channel is less direct than the theory. He would treat it as a serious alternative if the Committee judged the overlap not disqualifying.
responses.response: I keep B034 as my second alternative, with Kiyotaki and Moore only, but your two objections are fair and they are why it stays behind B001 and B006. The 2022 prize concerned banks, runs and the amplification of financial crises. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns how collateral constraints on borrowers propagate and amplify shocks over the cycle. That is distinguishable, and a citation tied to the dynamic collateral-constraint mechanism would make it clearer. It is also adjacent, and the Committee should not pretend otherwise. I agree that the empirical identification of the collateral channel is indirect compared with the firm-level tests that confirmed core B001 predictions. As a macroeconomist I may be somewhat generous to this mechanism, so I give your evidential-maturity point real weight.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg accepts B006's maturity and the clean BLP demand credit, but her reservation is evidentiary. Structural IO conclusions rest on functional-form and instrument assumptions, she asks about out-of-sample validation such as merger retrospectives, and she would reconsider if B006 were narrowed to the demand-estimation core.
responses.response: I think the evidentiary question is the right one to ask of B006, and I cannot answer it from the supplied evidence. I have not verified how well merger-simulation predictions have held up against retrospective outcomes. I would not dismiss B006 on that ground, since its use in practice and in trade, health and environmental applications gives it a record that is hard to ignore. But I agree it differs from B001, where the central selection and sorting predictions were directly testable in firm microdata and survived, with detailed failures that led to extensions. If the Committee wants to take B006 forward, I would support your suggestion of narrowing it to the demand-estimation core, and I would want the Scientific Background to state the validation evidence plainly.

responses.point: Friberg treats B006 as the strongest alternative and says that if the Bernard-Eaton-Kortum-Jensen parallel work is too entangled for a clean citation, he would move toward B006. He also keeps Redding's work as a separate quantitative-trade achievement (B037), and he discloses that his work is adjacent to trade and industrial organisation.
responses.response: I agree with the trigger you name, and it is the one I would use too: the strength of the attribution objection decides whether B001 holds. I also share your view that the quantitative-trade lineage is better judged as a separate achievement than folded into B001 as a third name. One further point of disclosure applies to us both. We co-authored the menu-cost paper, and you work close to the fields of both B001 and B006. I do not think that shifts either of us, but the Committee should know I am weighing your argument alongside a co-author's. For that reason I rest my reply on the attribution logic above and not on our shared view of the field.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not credited on this entry, as acknowledgeable in the background and citation wording or as making a two-name award too narrow. This is the main risk to my configuration.

Whether the discovery should be read as the selection and reallocation framework (Helpman and Melitz) or as the broader firm-level and quantitative-trade programme, in which case Redding's claim would rise and the credited set might change.

Whether B006 can be given a defensible boundary (demand estimation only versus the dynamic-games strand, and the roles of Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin), and how much out-of-sample validation exists for structural IO methods. I have not verified this.

How to weigh a conceptual reorientation of a field against a widely used toolkit with clean attribution. I treat the two as different kinds of contribution and not as ranked by rule, so the gap between B001 and B006 is small and judgement-dependent.

How far the sensitivity of the baseline model's welfare results to distributional assumptions should limit the citation. I would keep the wording to selection and reallocation and avoid claiming welfare magnitudes.
Whether the overlap of Helpman's earlier work with the lineage recognised in 2008 reduces the incremental novelty of this prize. I judge firm selection to be a distinct step.
My assessment rests on the supplied evidence and general knowledge. I have not independently verified citation counts, priority records or award history.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure, not adjudicated. No tie to Helpman, Melitz or Redding is apparent from my supplied profile, and none of my research is among the shortlisted discoveries. Ties to committee colleagues: I am an IIES colleague and long-term co-author of Per Krusell (committee secretary), I have co-authored with Timo Boppart, and I co-authored a menu-cost paper with Richard Friberg. None of them is a credited name on B001, B006 or B034, and I responded to Friberg above with this in mind. I gave the 2018 presentation speech, and the 2018 Scientific Background cites my own 2014 work, but these concern a different subject and I do not think they bear on trade. Whether I drafted parts of that background is not documented. I also prepared the round-1 chair summary, so I wrote the synthesis of colleagues' positions that I am now responding to. As a macroeconomist working with quantitative general-equilibrium models, I may be somewhat favourable to B001 (reallocation models) and to B034 (a macro mechanism), and I note that thematic proximity. Presentation speeches for the Academy may reflect collective drafting and do not establish my private preferences.
